title: Flood Insurance Claims Process in Galveston: NFIP Guide
description: A step-by-step guide to the NFIP flood insurance claims process in Galveston: reporting, proof of loss, elevated home limits, ICC coverage, and appeals.
html:
When storm surge or heavy rain puts water in your Galveston home, the flood insurance claims process runs on a different track than your homeowners or TWIA windstorm claim. Most flood policies here are written through the National Flood Insurance Program (NFIP), managed by FEMA and sold and serviced by private insurance companies. The rules are federal, the paperwork is strict, and the deadlines are real. This guide walks through each step so you know what to expect and where claims commonly go wrong.

How the Flood Insurance Claims Process Works

At a high level, an NFIP claim follows these stages:

  1. You report the loss to the company that services your flood policy.
  2. An independent adjuster is assigned and inspects the property.
  3. The adjuster prepares an estimate and, typically, a proof of loss.
  4. You review, sign and submit a proof of loss supporting the amount you are claiming.
  5. The insurer pays, partially pays, or denies all or part of the claim in writing.
  6. If you disagree, you can supplement the claim, appeal to FEMA, or pursue other remedies within the policy's time limits.

Each step has details that matter, especially on the island.

Step 1: Report the Flood Claim Quickly

Call your flood insurer or agent as soon as you can. You will need your policy number, the address, and a phone number where you can be reached. Write down the claim number and the name of everyone you speak with.

If you also have wind damage, report that separately to TWIA or your wind carrier. TWIA claims must be reported within one year of the date of loss, but there is no benefit to waiting. See our TWIA claims help page for that side of the loss.

Step 2: Document Before You Clean Up

Flood damage has to be proven, and much of it gets thrown away within days. Before you haul anything to the curb:

  • Photograph and video every room, including the high-water line on interior and exterior walls, with a tape measure in the frame
  • Photograph serial numbers and model plates on appliances, HVAC units and water heaters
  • Keep small samples of flooring, carpet, and drywall when practical
  • List damaged contents with approximate age and replacement cost
  • Save receipts for pumps, fans, dehumidifiers, and mitigation services

Start drying out quickly. Mold grows fast in Galveston heat, and NFIP policies expect you to take reasonable steps to protect the property.

Step 3: The Adjuster Inspection

The flood adjuster is usually an independent adjuster working on behalf of the insurer. They will measure, photograph, and prepare an estimate. Be present if you can, walk them through every damaged area, and point out damage that is easy to miss, such as wet insulation inside walls, damaged ductwork, and electrical components that were submerged.

Ask the adjuster for a copy of their estimate. You are entitled to understand how the number was calculated.

Step 4: The Proof of Loss

The proof of loss is the heart of the NFIP flood insurance claims process. It is your sworn statement of the amount you are claiming, and NFIP policies generally require it within 60 days of the date of loss. After large disasters FEMA sometimes extends that deadline, but you should never assume an extension applies to you without confirming it in writing.

The adjuster often prepares a proof of loss for you based on their estimate. You do not have to accept their figure if you believe it is too low. You can submit your own documented amount. For a full walk-through, see our blog guide to the sworn proof of loss.

What NFIP Covers and What Surprises Galveston Owners

Coverage limits

Residential NFIP policies have separate limits for the building and for contents, with federal maximums of $250,000 for a residential building and $100,000 for residential contents. Your actual limits are on your declarations page and may be lower. Contents coverage is only available if you purchased it.

Below the lowest elevated floor

Many Galveston homes are elevated on piers or pilings. NFIP coverage for enclosures and items below the lowest elevated floor is limited. Finished walls, flooring, and most contents in a ground-level enclosure are typically not covered, while certain essential equipment such as furnaces, water heaters, electrical panels and some foundation elements may be. Know this before the storm, and document these items carefully after one.

Replacement cost versus actual cash value

Some primary residences may qualify for replacement cost on the building. Contents are generally paid at actual cash value, meaning depreciation is subtracted. Check which applies to your policy.

Increased Cost of Compliance (ICC)

If your community determines your home is substantially damaged, you may be required to elevate, floodproof, relocate or demolish it. ICC coverage, which is part of standard NFIP building policies, can pay up to $30,000 toward those compliance costs, in addition to the building claim. Ask about ICC early if your damage is severe. Our Galveston local code page covers how local rules factor in.

Step 5: Payment, Partial Denial, or Denial

After review, you will receive payment, a partial payment, or a written denial of some or all of the claim. Read any denial letter carefully. It should explain the reason, such as damage attributed to a cause other than flood, items not covered below the lowest elevated floor, pre-existing damage, or a missing proof of loss.

Mortgage holders are often named on flood payments, so expect checks to be issued jointly with your lender for building damage.

Step 6: If You Disagree

You have several options if you believe your flood claim was underpaid:

  • Supplemental claim. If you find additional damage or have new documentation, you can ask to reopen or supplement the claim with a new proof of loss.
  • FEMA appeal. NFIP policyholders can appeal a claim decision to FEMA, generally within 60 days of the date of the written denial.
  • Lawsuit. NFIP claims have a strict deadline to file suit, generally one year from the date of the written denial of all or part of the claim.

These deadlines are short and unforgiving. Put them on your calendar the day you receive any letter.

Flood Insurance Claims Process Checklist

  • Report the claim and record the claim number
  • Photograph the water line, every room, and serial numbers
  • Start drying and save mitigation receipts
  • Separate damage above and below the lowest elevated floor
  • Get the adjuster's estimate in writing
  • Submit a documented proof of loss before the deadline
  • Ask about ICC if the home may be substantially damaged
  • File any wind or TWIA claim separately
  • Calendar appeal and lawsuit deadlines from any denial letter

How a Public Adjuster Helps With a Flood Claim

A licensed public adjuster (in Texas, licensed by the Texas Department of Insurance) represents the policyholder. On a flood claim, that can mean preparing a detailed estimate, organizing the contents inventory, handling the proof of loss, and coordinating the flood claim with the wind claim so damage is not left in the gap between two insurers. We do not promise a particular outcome, but we help make sure your claim is complete and on time. You can also review Galveston's history of surge events on our storm history page.

If you are in the middle of the flood insurance claims process and the numbers do not look right, talk to us before the deadlines pass. faq.q: How long do I have to file a proof of loss on an NFIP flood claim?
faq.a: NFIP policies generally require a signed proof of loss within 60 days of the date of loss. FEMA sometimes extends this after major disasters, but confirm any extension in writing before relying on it.

faq.q: Is my ground-level enclosure covered by flood insurance?
faq.a: Coverage below the lowest elevated floor of an elevated home is limited. Finished walls, flooring and most contents there are typically not covered, while certain essential equipment and foundation elements may be. Check your policy.

faq.q: Can I appeal a flood claim decision?
faq.a: Yes. NFIP policyholders can appeal to FEMA, generally within 60 days of the written denial, and there is a separate deadline, generally one year from the written denial, to file a lawsuit.
